summary:
Bayern stands under Germany's national framework on legal gender recognition, identity documents, relationship recognition and anti-discrimination, and that layer is carried by the national record. What follows is specific to the Free State.

A prohibition on gender-inclusive German took effect in Bavaria on 1 April 2024. It bars gender-neutral word forms in schools, universities and all state administration, implementing a government declaration of December 2023 together with a cabinet decision amending the language rules that govern public authorities. Critics dismiss the measure as symbol politics while pointing out that it reaches every public counter, registry office and classroom in the state. A trans visitor dealing with a Bavarian registry office, town hall or university therefore deals with offices operating under an official register from which gender-neutral wording has been excluded.

Bavaria has co-sponsored a Bundesrat initiative with Sachsen, Thüringen and Sachsen-Anhalt to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act, an organised Land-level attempt to make the nationwide self-declaration route stricter. The contested ground behind the initiative was the Act's treatment of children's gender entry: the Bundesrat's criticism of 20 October 2023 held that the draft allowed parents to decide changes for under-14s "without any counselling, examination and investigation of the child's welfare". The Free State government's posture toward self-declaration is therefore openly restrictive, even though the procedure itself remains the national one.
tangentialFactors:
The language ban is one of two organised Bavarian interventions in the national gender-recognition debate; the other is the four-state Bundesrat initiative, in which Bavaria acts alongside Sachsen, Thüringen and Sachsen-Anhalt. No source in the inventory records comparable legislative activity by the Free State on documents, facilities, healthcare or custody.

The ban's critics and its authors agree on its reach and disagree only on its value: the government treats gender-inclusive German as a matter for state language rules, while opponents characterise the measure as symbolic. The disagreement does not change the practical scope, which covers administration, education and public-facing counters alike.
localsOnly:
For people living in Bavaria, the language restriction binds schools, universities and the entire state administration. Public-sector employees and students must use a prescribed register of German, and the rules were adopted through the state cabinet rather than by a vote in the Landtag.

The Free State's executive has made restriction of the national self-declaration procedure a position it carries into the Bundesrat, joining three other Länder in seeking tighter conditions on legal gender change. Residents of Bavaria are subject to the national procedure in force, but the state government's stated objective is a stricter version of it.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the four-Länder initiative produced any amendment to the national procedure, or any change in how Bavarian registry offices apply it, is not sourced here.

Unresolved: no information in the inventory addresses whether the language prohibition affects how Bavarian registry offices record, display or speak about a changed gender entry or name on documents issued in the Free State.

Not sourced: Bavaria-specific reporting on prison placement, airport or transport screening, access to gendered facilities, healthcare refusal, hate-crime incidents or protection machinery. The national record carries that material; no Free State figure or case appears in this inventory.
